newsitem.title: USA: After "jusen" bail-out, Japan banks may go Western.
newsitem.headline: After "jusen" bail-out, Japan banks may go Western.

text.p: Japan's banking system is not likely to suffer a meltdown, especially now that the Japanese government has stepped in to bail out debt-ridden housing lenders, said experts at a conference on the future of Japan's banking system which took place on Wednesday.

But financial deregulation, in the wake of the political backlash to the rescue, may soon prod Japan's banks to model themselves after U.S. and European financial institutions, speakers at New York's Japan Society gathering said.
"Japanese banks, if they hope to play in global markets, must adopt a more Western style of management," said Akira Kondoh, director and general manager of Sumitomo Bank Ltd in New York.

The recent passing of legislation to prop-up the housing loan corporations -- or jusen -- barely puts a dent in the bad loan problem, which has rocked Japan's financial markets and shaken global investors.
But the banks have deep enough pockets to absorb these non-performing loans, experts said.
"This is not a debilitating problem, it's not going to take down the whole financial structure," said Ethan Penner, president Nomura Asset Capital Corporation.
Estimates of non-performing loans haunting balance sheets of Japan's financial institutions range from $100 billion to $450 billion, experts said.

Public anger over the taxpayer bailout and at the bankers has prompted various plans for reform, restructuring and further deregulation. It has also led the Ministry of Finance, which regulates banking, to draw up a reorganization plan, the unveiling of which is expected any day.

Just as the Depression-era walls separating banking and securities underwriting in the U.S. slowly crumble, the division between investment banking and commercial banking in Japan may be reviewed again, said experts.
"Basically, I think we need more deregulation of the industries," said Shuzo Nakamura, Deputy Consul General and Head of Finance Division, at Japan's New York consulate.
"The banks need to compete better with other financial industries...and other industries need ... to have access to the things that are normally allowed to banks," he said.

Nakamura said in the past Japanese securities firms have had limited access to the foreign exchange markets, which have been the domain of large commercial banks. At the same time banks need access to capital markets so they can compete better with the securities firms.
The Japanese parliament may take up measures to aid the lowering of some barriers in 1997.
Legislation to further relax regulation on foreign exchange markets is being drafted and may be submitted to the Diet next year for approval, Nakamura said.
